prompt: In many communities, local charities and clubs are finding it increasingly difficult to recruit volunteers. Why is this happening? What could be done to encourage more people to give their time?
essay:
Charities and clubs that struggle to recruit volunteers often conclude that people have become less willing to help. The response to any local emergency suggests otherwise. What has declined is not generosity but a particular kind of commitment — the same evening every week, indefinitely — and that is precisely the kind most local organisations are still built around.

Three changes have made that commitment harder to give. For many people, working hours are less predictable than they were: someone whose shifts are published a week in advance cannot honestly promise to run a youth club every Tuesday. People also move more often, for work or for cheaper rent, so fewer of them expect to stay anywhere long enough to put down roots, and the word-of-mouth recruitment that once filled a rota passes them by. And volunteering has acquired some of the machinery of employment — induction sessions, background checks, policies to sign — which is sensible for someone coaching children but deters someone who simply offered to help at a summer fair.

If the problem is the shape of the commitment, the remedy is to change the shape. Organisations that break roles into single sessions or short projects, bookable online like any other appointment, can draw on people whose weeks have no fixed Tuesday. Checks can be scaled to risk, so that the volunteer who serves tea at a lunch club is not vetted like the one who is left alone with a child. Employers can help at the source by granting a few days of paid volunteering leave a year. And for people who move often, a record of volunteering that travels with them, recognised by organisations in the next town, would make each move an introduction rather than a fresh start.

None of this will restore the older model, and it should not be expected to. The steady weekly volunteer, often retired, still holds many organisations together, and that loyalty deserves protecting. But a charity that can only use people able to give it the same evening every week has limited itself to a pool of helpers that is shrinking, and it has usually done so out of habit rather than necessity.
title: Why local charities struggle to find volunteers
